name: Path Locative-Complement Construction

dimensions.form: Verb head with a path-denoting PP in locative-complement function
dimensions.meaning: Intermediate location or route traversed during motion, without itself necessarily specifying either terminal point
dimensions.function: Locative complement of the verb, bearing the semantic role path
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal with motion verbs and motion construals; compatible with separate source- and goal-role complements

1.definition: A VP contains a locative PP complement that identifies the route or intermediate location traversed by the moving theme
1.details: Path is a semantic role, while locative complement is the CGEL syntactic function. Via uniquely marks path in its central spatial use, and along is strongly path-associated. PPs headed by across, through, up, and similar prepositions can instead express location, source, or goal; a path construal identifies an intermediate portion of a larger trajectory. Path complements are integrated into the motion VP and fall within do so scope (CGEL Ch. 8 §4.3, pp. 684–88).

examples.note: Via-PP with an unambiguous spatial-path role
Along-PP identifying a route without a terminal point

examples.form: They [walked from the station up the hill to the new Civic Centre].
examples.note: Path up the hill occurs between separate source and goal complements

constraints.description: The path PP is an integrated locative complement in a motion VP, not a clause-level location adjunct.
The PP identifies the route or an intermediate location; it need not identify the initial or final location.
A path complement normally leaves the motion unbounded and therefore permits a for-duration phrase; a syncretic path-goal reading can instead bound the event and license an in-duration phrase.
Source, path, and goal may be separately realized in one VP; their co-occurrence does not impose an invariant surface order.
This entry establishes V-hosted path complementation only; it makes no claim that a path PP is selected inside a larger PP without independent attachment evidence.

projection.target: Identifying an integrated PP as a path complement predicts an intermediate-location interpretation, compatibility with separate source and goal complements, and absence of event bounding unless the PP simultaneously receives a goal construal
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts path and goal readings by terminal-point entailments and in/for duration, identifies via and along as central path markers, and shows paths co-occurring between source and goal (Ch. 8 §4.3, pp. 684–88).

core.property: Path role borne by a locative PP complement

diagnostics: compatibility with an overt following goal

known_boundary_items: ran across the bridge: across the bridge can be goal when it supplies the final location, or path when a later goal is expressed
walked through the forest in eight hours: the in-duration phrase selects a goal construal in which the end of the forest is reached
A location adjunct describes where the situation occurs; a path complement describes the trajectory of the moving theme and is included in do so scope
No PP-internal path-complement attachment is asserted by this VP-level entry

curious.title: Naming the route of a journey
curious.summary: Some verbs of moving are followed by a phrase that says which way the traveller went, without saying where the journey started or ended.
curious.body:
In She came via the bridge, the phrase via the bridge tells us the route. It names a place along the way, not the starting point or the destination. In They strolled along the castle wall, the same thing happens: we learn the route and nothing about where the stroll ended.

This dictionary calls that role the path. A route phrase can sit in the same sentence as a starting point and a destination, as in They walked from the station up the hill to the new Civic Centre, where up the hill is the middle stretch. Via and along are strongly tied to routes, but a phrase starting with across, through or up can name a place, a starting point or a destination instead, depending on the sentence.

examples.text: They [walked from the station up the hill to the new Civic Centre].

curious.try: Think of a trip you made. Which words in your sentence name the route, and which name where you started or finished?

teacher.summary: Helps students tell route phrases (path) from starting-point and destination phrases after verbs of motion.
teacher.explain: In a motion VP, a PP in locative-complement function can bear the semantic role path: the route or intermediate location the moving thing traverses. Path is a role; locative complement is the syntactic function. Via marks path in its central spatial use, and along is strongly path-associated. PPs with across, through or up can instead express location, source or goal. A path complement normally leaves the motion unbounded, so it permits a for-duration phrase; a reading that also bounds the event can license an in-duration phrase. Source, path and goal can all appear in one VP, with no fixed surface order. A path complement is part of the VP, unlike a location adjunct, and it falls within do so scope.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes group these with adverbials of place or direction. In this grammar, path is a semantic role and locative complement is the syntactic function.

examples.text: They [walked from the station up the hill to the new Civic Centre].

contrasts.text: They walked through the forest for hours.
contrasts.note: A for-duration phrase fits when the PP names a route and the motion has no endpoint.

contrasts.text: They walked through the forest in eight hours.
contrasts.note: An in-duration phrase selects a reading where the end of the forest is reached, so the PP also supplies a goal.

watch_for: A learner might read every PP after a motion verb as the destination, when up the hill in the station-to-Civic-Centre example names the middle of the journey.
A learner might assume across or through marks a route every time, though they can also express location, source or goal.
teacher.activity: Give pairs a short map with a start, a destination and two landmarks. Each pair writes one sentence naming the route only, then one adding the start and the destination. They underline the phrase that names the route.
